Supplementation of KOH to improve salt tolerance of methanogenesis in 
the two-stage anaerobic digestion of food waste using pre-acclimated 
anaerobically digested sludge by air-nanobubble water 
Tingting Hou , Jiamin Zhao , Zhongfang Lei , Kazuya Shimizu , Zhenya Zhang * 
Graduate School of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8572, Japan   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• ETS 
activity 
of 
AD 
sludge 
pre- 
acclimated by Air-NBW was enhanced 
3.4 times. 
• H2 yield was increased by 46% in the 
NBW group.

A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
High saline food waste 
Air-nanobubble water 
Two-stage anaerobic digestion 
KOH 
A B S T R A C T   
Air-nanobubble water (NBW) was applied to pre-acclimate anaerobically digested sludge that was then used as 
the inoculum in the two-stage anaerobic digestion (AD) of high saline (20 g NaCl/L) food waste (FW) to optimize 
NBW application in the AD of high saline FW. K+ was simultaneously supplemented during the methanogenic 
stage to resist the inhibition of salt on methanogens. Results showed that after the second pre-acclimation cycle, 
the inoculum activity was increased 27% in the Air-NBW supplemented reactor in comparison to the deionized 
water (DW) supplemented one. In the first-stage AD, H2 yield was enhanced by 46% in the Air-NBW pre-accli­
mated sludge reactor compared with the DW pre-acclimated sludge reactor. Besides, supplementation of KOH in 
the methanogenic stage could enhance methane production by 17–25% in the DW reactors at initial pH 7.5, 8.0, 
and 9.0 when compared to the control reactor (using NaOH adjusted initial pH to 7.5), respectively.   
1. Introduction 
Salinity is one of the most stressful abiotic factors that limit hydrogen 
and/or methane production in the anaerobic digestion (AD) process, 
which has attracted much attention of researchers. On the other hand, 
food waste (FW) is becoming an increasingly preferred feedstock for AD, 
which normally contains a high salinity because salt is extensively used 
as a food flavoring agent, especially in Japan. Asakura et al. (2014) 
pointed out that a much higher level of Na+ than the world health or­
ganization (WHO) recommendation was consumed by most Japanese 
due to the Japanese diet. As known, high salinity (>10 g NaCl/L) usually 
increases the osmotic pressure outside the cells and causes the outflow of 
intracellular water or even the cell rupture, which strongly inhibits the 
metabolism of non-halophilic bacteria (Li et al., 2018). Therefore,

excessive salt present in organic wastes, i.e., FW, could inhibit the ac­
tivities of microorganisms in all stages (hydrolysis/acidification and 
methanogenesis) of AD to varying degrees, resulting in a lower AD 
performance and even process failure. Among them, high salinity may 
more remarkably inhibit methane production than hydrogen and vola­
tile fatty acids (VFAs) production because the methanogens are more 
sensitive to environmental factors like high salt concentration than the 
hydrolytic bacteria (Wang et al., 2018a). Additionally, it has been found 
that anaerobic microbes need some time to accommodate the hypersa­
line environments when dealing with the highly saline FW, which is 
probably the main reason for a longer startup time (about 20 days) at 20 
g NaCl/L in a previous study (Hou et al., 2021b). Hierholtzer and 
Akunna (2014) also found a similar phenomenon that methane pro­
duction was delayed by about 15 days in the AD of saline-rich macro­
algae system. These observations suggest that high salinity could 
strongly inhibit microbial activity during the early stage of methano­
genesis. Therefore, some strategies for addressing this problem though 
improving microbial activity are recommended. 
In general, the tolerance of microorganisms to high salinity could be 
improved by the synthesis of themselves or adding external osmopro­
tectants, allowing microorganisms to accumulate osmolytes (compatible 
solutes) and balance their cytoplasms (Salma et al., 2020). Amino acids 
and quaternary ammonium compounds, including proline, choline, 
glycine betaine, carnitine, and trehalose, have been adopted as common 
osmoprotectants in the AD of high saline organic wastes to recover 
methanogenic activity and increase methane production (Oh et al., 
2008; Liu et al., 2019b; Zhang et al., 2016). However, Liu et al. (2019b) 
reported that excessive addition of osmoprotectants had an adverse ef­
fect on methane production. Apart from this, the osmoprotectants are 
organic substances that may be consumed by microorganisms as carbon 
or nitrogen sources, resulting in instability in continuous AD systems. 
Therefore, seeking other methods to improve the methanogens activity 
in a high salt environment is necessary. Most recently, some researchers 
had reported that the nanobubble water (NBW) (the water containing 
bubbles with the diameter <1000 nm) has the unique characteristics 
including negative charge on their surfaces, high mass transfer effi­
ciency, and large specific surface area of NBs, which may facilitate the 
chemical reaction, physical adsorption, and mass transport at the gas- 
liquid interface (Gurung et al., 2016). Therefore, adding NBW in AD 
system as a novel strategy has been put forward and demonstrated to 
enhance the bioactivities of enzymes involving in the AD systems, 
including hydrolases, cellulase, and coenzyme F420 (Hou et al., 2021a; 
Hou et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2020a). According to previous studies, 
however, the volume of NBW-based AD reactors is relatively large, 
which could increase the construction costs. On the contrary, if the 
anaerobically digested sludge is firstly acclimated by NBW and then 
used as the inoculum to the AD system, not only the activity of micro­
organisms can be enhanced, but also the volume of reactors may be 
largely reduced when compared to that with NBW being added directly. 
On the other hand, salinity can induce K+ efflux from cells, causing 
osmotic pressure imbalance and ultimately cell lysis and death because 
K+ is an essential element for regulating intracellular osmotic pressure 
(Larbi et al., 2020; Plemenitas et al., 2014). Meanwhile, K+ as a favor­
able alternative osmolyte in cells can be transported through the unique 
potassium pump system on the cell membrane (Zhang et al., 2016). 
Therefore, supplementation of K+ as an accelerator may provide a new 
train of thought for improving the biological treatment process of high 
saline wastes. Gul et al. (2019) reported that the moderately supple­
mented K+ reduced the concentration of Na+ in tissues and cells and 
alleviated the deleterious effects of Na+ toxicity on the wheat growth 
and yield. Gan et al. (2021) also found that the proportion of genus 
Lactobacillus was increased from 22% (fresh meat) to 73%, 82%, 77% 
and 86% at the end of processing when NaCl was partially replaced with 
0%, 30%, 50%, and 70% of KCl. It is noteworthy that addition of 0.174% 
KCl to the AD of saline organic wastewater increased methane produc­
tion by about 49% when the NaCl content was 2.0% (Li et al., 2018). The 
residual digestate slurry at the end of hydrolysis/acidification stage is 
always weakly acidic from the two-stage AD of FW. When it is used as 
the substrate for the methanogenic stage, proper adjustment of pH value 
using bases such as NaOH is necessary in order to meet the suitable 
growth environment for methanogens. Therefore, substitution of NaOH 
with KOH as a pH regulator may not only reduce the additional increase 
in Na+ but also mitigate the toxicity of high salinity on methanogens 
during the AD of high saline organic wastes due to the supplemented K+. 
This study was conducted in two steps to eliminate the adverse ef­
fects of high salt concentration (20 g NaCl/L) on two-stage AD of FW. 
Firstly, the anaerobically digested sludge was acclimated by using Air- 
NBW or deionized water (DW) (as control) and then the acclimated 
sludge was used as inoculum during the two-stage AD of FW system. 
Secondly, KOH was added to adjust the pH at the beginning of meth­
anogenic stage to 7.5, 8.0, and 9.0, respectively, and then the effects of 
different K+ dosages on methanogens under the high salt concentration 
by using the DW or Air-NBW pre-acclimated anaerobically digested 
sludge were examined. This study is expected to develop a feasible 
strategy for the practical application of Air-NBW and offer novel insights 
into the improvement of salt tolerance of anaerobic microorganisms in 
the two-stage AD of high saline organic wastes. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Anaerobically digested sludge, feedstock, and Air-NBW 
Anaerobically digested sludge was gained from the anaerobic 
bioreactor of Chikusai wastewater treatment center in Ibaraki, Japan. 
The initial total solid (TS) and volatile solid (VS) of the raw sludge were 
0.88 ± 0.04% and 0.58 ± 0.05%, indicating its high moisture content 
(Table 1). Therefore, the sludge was concentrated through a 1 mm pore 
size sieve and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 15 min. The TS and VS of the 
concentrated sludge were 2.45 ± 0.02% and 1.92 ± 0.02%. In this study, 
synthetic FW was used, which was the same as reported in a previous 
study (Hou et al., 2021b). The main physicochemical characteristics of 
FW and raw anaerobically digested sludge are also described in Table 1. 
For the manufacturing process of Air-NBW, a NBW generator (HACK 
FB11, Japan) with the pressure of 0.22–0.25 MPa and the flow rates of 
gas and water of 0.05 L/min and 3 L/min was used, which was based on 
the previous study (Hou et al., 2021b). After 20 min generation time, the 
number of bubble particles was around 3×108 particles/mL with the 
particle size ranging from 59 to 127 nm. 
2.2. Pre-acclimation of anaerobically digested sludge by DW or Air-NBW 
Inoculum plays a pivotal role in the anaerobic biological process 
because the stability and efficiency of AD have a strong correlation with 
the number, species, and metabolic activities of microorganisms (Fran­
chi et al., 2018). In this study, the anaerobically digested sludge with the 
initial electron transport system (ETS) activity of 19.87 ± 0.63 mg/(g⋅h) 
was pre-acclimated by Air-NBW, which was expected to improve the 
microbial activity and help microorganisms resist the toxicity of high 
salt.

g FW (wet weight) at a substrate to inoculum ratio (S/I) (VS basis) of 0.5 
were added into each 500 mL digester, and then DW or Air-NBW was 
used to adjust its working volume to 350 mL. Each reactor was purged 
by pure N2 for 2 min, 3 times and the initial pH was 6.79 ± 0.42 in the 
first cycle and 7.51 ± 0.12 in the second cycle with no additional 
adjustment. All the digesters were placed at a constant temperature of 
38 ± 1◦C. At the end of test, the reaction slurry was concentrated again 
through the 1 mm pore size sieve and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 15 
min, which was then utilized as the inoculum in the second cycle to 
repeat the above acclimation procedure. During the two cycles of 
acclimation, methane production was measured every two days and ETS 
activity was detected at the end of each cycle (around one month). 
2.3. Two-stage AD of high saline FW by using Air-NBW pre-acclimated 
anaerobically digested sludge as inoculum 
2.3.1. Performance of the first-stage AD 
Hydrogen production potential tests were carried out in 100 mL re­
actors, and the working volume of each bottle was 55 mL. 15 g (wet 
weight) of FW together with the 20 g/L of salt (NaCl) concentration and 
40 mL of above pre-acclimated anaerobically digested sludge as inoc­
ulum were added to each reactor. A higher initial total VS about 6% was 
achieved in each reactor, and the S/I ratio was approximately 6.0 (VS 
basis). No additional chemical reagents were added to adjust the pH 
during the first stage. Although FW had a low pH of 4.30, the initial pH 
in each reactor was 6.50 ± 0.20 after all the above procedures being 
completed, which was within the appropriate pH range for hydrogen 
production. The reactors were labelled as DW and Air-NBW according to 
the water added during the pre-acclimation stage. 
2.3.2. Effect of KOH addition on the performance of the second-stage AD 
For methane production potential tests, the reactors with the same 
specifications as in the first stage were used with the same working 
volume of 55 mL each. The residual acidified slurry from the first stage 
and the pre-acclimated anaerobically digested sludge were respectively 
added as substrate and inoculum in each reactor (at the S/I ratio of 2 (VS 
basis)). The initial total VS in each reactor was 1.9 ± 0.02%. Afterwards, 
in order to evaluate the effects of KOH as an accelerator on methane 
production from the AD of high saline FW, the initial pH of each reactor 
was adjusted to 7.5, 8.0, and 9.0 using 6 M KOH, respectively. The initial 
pH of the control group was adjusted to 7.5 by using 6 M NaOH. And 
these reactors were designated as DWcontrol-7.5, DW-7.5, DW-8.0, DW- 
9.0, NBWcontrol-7.5, NBW-7.5, NBW-8.0, and NBW-9.0, respectively. 
Each reactor was hermetically sealed and purged with pure N2 for 2 
min, 3 times to maintain the anaerobic condition in all experiments prior 
to start and then placed in a constant temperature incubator (38 ± 1◦C). 
Biogas production was measured regularly at room pressure (25◦C, 1 
atm) and the contents of hydrogen and methane were checked by a gas 
chromatograph (GC-8A, Shimadzu, Japan). 
2.4. Analytical methods and calculations 
The contents of TS, VS, and alkalinity including total alkalinity (TA), 
partial alkalinity (PA, endpoint pH to 5.75), and intermediate alkalinity 
(IA, pH from 5.75 to 4.30) were based on the standard methods (APHA, 
2012). A semi-solid pH meter (Testo 206, Germany) was used to monitor 
the pH value. In addition, the liquid samples were centrifuged at 9900 
rpm for 20 min and filtrated through 0.22 μm membrane filters to 
determine the concentrations of soluble protein, soluble carbohydrate, 
VFA, and lactic acid. Among them, the concentration of soluble protein, 
carbohydrate, and VFAs were determined according to a previous study 
(Hou et al., 2020). Lactic acid was quantified by using a spectropho­
tometer (Shimadzu, Japan) according to Borshchevskaya et al. (2016). 
For the determination of concentrations of NH4

trogen, TAN) and K+, the samples were filtered through 0.22 μm filters 
and then measured by Ion Chromatography (IC, Shimadzu, Japan). Free 
ammonia nitrogen (FAN) was calculated according to the following Eq.

The microbial activities during the two-stage AD were reflected by 
the electron transport rate, i.e., ETS activity. The 2-(p-iodophenyl)-3-(p- 
nitrophenyl)-5-phenyltetrazolium chloride-electron transport system 
(INT-ETS) reduction method was used. The specific procedures were 
based on the report by Wang et al. (2020a). 0.1 mL of 0.2% INT solution 
was added to 0.5 mL of samples, and the centrifuge tubes were incubated 
in a water bath oscillator at 100 rpm and 37 ± 1◦C for 30 min under dark 
conditions. The reaction was then terminated with 1 mL of 37% meth­
anol, and the reactants were centrifuged at 10000 rpm, 4◦C for 5 min 
before the supernatant was discarded. Subsequently, 5 mL of 98% 
methanol was added to the sediment to shake in the same water bath 
oscillator again for 10 min under a dark environment. Then, the su­
pernatants were obtained after centrifugation (10000 rpm, 4◦C for 5 
min) and determined by a spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, Japan) at 485 
nm. Finally, the sediments were dried to constant weight at 105 ± 1◦C. 
The kinetic analysis by using the modified Gompertz model was carried 
as mentioned previously (Hou et al., 2021a). 
2.5. Data calculation and analysis 
All the reactors operation were performed in duplicate with triplicate 
measurements for each sample. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) 
was conducted to probe the statistical difference via Microsoft Office 
Excel 2010, and statistical significance was assumed at p < 0.05. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. CH4 yield and ETS activity during the pre-acclimation process 
Microorganisms with robust physiology are essential for the stable 
performance of AD. When fed with a new substrate, the established 
consortium of anaerobically digested sludge generally needs time to 
adapt to the new environment (V´asquez and Nakasaki, 2016). When FW 
is directly used as the substrate to the AD system, the imbalance 
occurred would lead to a slow start-up with a low efficiency (Zeng et al., 
2019). Therefore, some pre-acclimation of anaerobically digested sludge 
is necessary. In this study, the anaerobically digested sludge was pre- 
acclimated at a low S/I ratio by adding Air-NBW, so as to enhance the 
microbial activities of the inoculum and the performance of the two- 
stage AD of high saline FW. 
During the two cycles of pre-acclimation, the cumulative CH4 yields 
were examined, and the results are displayed in Fig. 1a. As seen, the 
cumulative CH4 yields in the Air-NBW reactor (169.88 ± 1.83 mL/g- 
VSadded in the first cycle and 217.46 ± 0.50 mL/g-VSadded in the second 
cycle) were higher around 14% and 33% than that in the DW reactor 
during both cycles, respectively. ETS activity also showed the similar 
results, which were increased by 0.9 and 1.2 times in the first cycle and 
2.5 and 3.4 times in the second cycle in the DW and Air-NBW pre- 
acclimated sludge reactor when compared to the raw anaerobically 
digested sludge (19.87 ± 0.63 mg/(g⋅h)), respectively (shown in 
Fig. 1b). This observation indicates that pre-acclimation of anaerobi­
cally digested sludge is an effective enhancement approach for microbial 
activity. After the second cycle, the highest ETS activity was detected in 
the Air-NBW reactor (87.03 mg/(g⋅h)), increasing by 27% when 
compared with that in the DW reactor. Xiao and Xu (2020) also found 
that use of NBs technology would achieve 6 times higher dehydrogenase 
activity than that of coarse bubbles, resulting in enhanced microbial 
metabolism and microorganisms’ proliferation. This finding agrees with 
Gurung et al. (2016) who stated that NBs technology possesses greater

application potentials in the field of environmental engineering because 
it can enhance biological activity and mass transfer efficiency to a great 
extent. Results from this study also suggested that anaerobically diges­
ted sludge pre-acclimated by Air-NBW exhibited a higher biological 
activity and methane production potential. 
3.2. Reactor performance at hydrolysis/acidification stage by using Air- 
NBW pre-acclimated anaerobically digested sludge as inoculum 
3.2.1. H2 yield and ETS activity 
The hourly H2 production, cumulative H2 yield, and ETS activity 
during the first stage are displayed in Fig. 2. The H2 production was 
completed within 48 h, indicating a quick start-up of the reactors. In 
particular, the hourly H2 production from the Air-NBW group was 
higher than that from the DW group during the whole stage, and the 
highest value was obtained at 12 h, about 29.45 ± 1.21 mL/g-VSadded. A 
previous study (Hou et al., 2021b) showed a lag time (λ) of 17.87 ± 1.30 
h at 20 g NaCl/L. Cao and Zhao (2009) also obtained the λ of 14.6 and 
29.2 h when the salt concentrations were 19.19 and 24.49 g NaCl/L, 
respectively. However, in this study no inhibition was observed at the 
high salinity of 20 g NaCl/L when the pre-acclimated sludge was used as 
inoculum. The λ was only 3.72 ± 0.06 h in the DW pre-acclimated sludge 
reactor and 2.90 ± 0.02 h in the Air-NBW pre-acclimated sludge reactor, 
respectively (Table 2). As shown in Fig. 2b, the cumulative H2 yield from 
the Air-NBW group was enhanced by 46% in comparison to the DW 
group. These data confirm that the performance of H2 production could 
be enhanced at the high salinity condition in the AD reactor inoculated 
with the Air-NBW pre-acclimated sludge. 
The changes of ETS activity at the first stage (Fig. 2b) were consistent 
with the results of hydrogen production, which can indirectly reflect the 
metabolic activity relating to electron transfer in microbial cells. High 
hydrogen production was accompanied by an increase in ETS activity, 
and the ETS activity in the Air-NBW group was always higher than that 
in the DW group. In particular, the ETS activities in the Air-NBW

h, respectively, suggesting the more excellent microbial metabolic ac­

the increased microbial biomass after being acclimated by Air-NBW. 
Zhao et al. (2020b) reported the increase in the diversity and abun­

3.2.2. Variation in VFAs and lactic acid concentration during the hydrogen 
fermentation 
Besides pH, the concentrations of VFAs and lactic acid were detected 
during the first stage (Fig. 3). Previous research proved the existent of 
different hydrogen-producing fermentation pathways (i.e., butyric acid 
(HBu)-type fermentation and mixed-acid fermentation) in anaerobic 
fermentation systems, which may lead to the accumulation of various 
end products (Lee et al., 2012). VFAs as the main by-product from H2 
production were accumulated rapidly in the first 12 h and after that a 
slow increase was observed (Fig. 3a). At the end of 48 h, the total VFA 
concentrations were 4189.30 ± 37.94 and 4948.41 ± 177.26 mg/L in 
the DW reactor and Air-NBW reactor, respectively. The concentration of 
HBu was about 33% higher in the Air-NBW reactor than that in the DW 
reactor, suggesting that the HBu-type fermentation was more dominant 
in the Air-NBW reactor. In addition, a high carbohydrates content 
(41–62%) in FW often leads to the accumulation of lactic acid, which is 
the main product of carbohydrate fermentation (Anna et al., 2013). 
However, the lactic acid concentration was not significantly different 
among the reactors during the first 6 h, and from 12 h on its concen­
tration in the DW reactor was always higher than that in the Air-NBW 
reactor (Fig. 3b). At the end of the first stage, the lactic acid concen­
trations were 9.50 ± 0.20 and 7.64 ± 0.16 g/L in the DW reactor and 
Air-NBW reactor, respectively. This indicates that the microbial com­
munity might shift toward lactic acid metabolism in the DW reactor, 
probably attributing to the decrease in hydrogen production. Ghimire 
et al. (2018) investigated the accumulation of lactic acid during 
hydrogen production and found that the decrease in hydrogen produc­
tion was related to the metabolic transfer caused by lactic acid accu­
mulation. Anna et al. (2013) summarized the reasons for the inhibition 
of hydrogen production by lactic acid, including the competition of 
lactic acid bacteria for substrates and the excretion of bacteriocins that 
can inhibit the growth of other microorganisms. In addition, the accu­
mulation of lactic acid also contributed to a lower pH in the DW group 
(Fig. 3b). At the end of the first stage, the pH values were 3.83 ± 0.01 
and 3.94 ± 0.03 in the DW group and the Air-NBW group, respectively. 
3.3. Effects of KOH addition on CH4 production from second-stage AD 
inoculated with Air-NBW pre-acclimated anaerobically digested sludge 
3.3.1. CH4 yield and ETS activity 
The CH4 production rate and cumulative CH4 yield during the second 
stage are displayed in Fig. 4. As shown, there is no significant difference 
in CH4 production among all the reactors during the first 6 days (p =
0.38 > 0.05). Notably, the reactors with the addition of KOH were 
started up faster than the control group, and the λ in the Air-NBW pre- 
acclimated sludge reactors were shorter than those in the DW pre- 
acclimated sludge reactors (Table 2). The CH4 production potential 
(PCH4) and CH4 production rate (RCH4, max) reflected the consistent re­
sults, with the highest PCH4 and RCH4, max being obtained in the NBW-8.0 
and NBW-9.0, respectively. As expected, the final cumulative CH4 yields 
(Fig. 4b) were about 22%, 25%, and 17% higher in the DW-7.5 (268.54 
± 1.83 mL/g-VSadded), DW-8.0 (275.39 ± 2.85 mL/g-VSadded), and DW- 
9.0 (258.09 ± 4.12 mL/g-VSadded) than that in the DWcontorl-7.5 (220.83 
± 1.44 mL/g-VSadded), respectively. Correspondingly, the final cumu­
lative CH4 yields were 19%, 26%, and 25% respectively higher in the 
NBW-7.5 (281.40 ± 1.12 mL/g-VSadded), NBW-8.0 (297.21 ± 3.86 mL/g- 
VSadded), and NBW-9.0 (295.87 ± 7.29 mL/g-VSadded) than that in the 
NBWcontorl-7.5 (236.79 ± 10.30 mL/g-VSadded). These results indicate 
that the addition of K+ can effectively alleviate the inhibition of high 
salinity on methane production. This observation may be associated 
with the fact that the supplementation of K+ could regulate the osmotic 
pressure in microbial cells and prevent the accumulation of Na+ in the 
cells so as to maintain a high cell survival rate (Tang et al., 2018). 
Additionally, a decline trend of methane yield was noticed with the 
increase of K+ dosage in the DW pre-acclimated sludge reactors, in 
agreement with Li et al. (2018) who found that excessive K+ had a 
negative effect on methane production. This phenomenon may be 
brought about by the toxicity of excessive salt concentration to micro­
bial activity (Ashfaq et al., 2020). However, the decline of methane yield 
was not obvious when the K+ dosage was increased by adjusting the pH 
to 9.0 in the NBW pre-acclimated reactors, indicating that the micro­
organisms would have a stronger tolerance to environmental toxicants 
after being acclimated by Air-NBW. This may be due to the increased 
microbial activity after the anaerobically digested sludge pre-acclimated 
by Air-NBW, which was consistent with the results of ETS activity 
(shown in Fig. 4c). 
As shown in Fig. 4c, the ETS activity in all the reactors was increased 
gradually during the first 24 days, in agreement with the methane 
production. It was clearly observed that the ETS activities in the K+
addition reactors were always higher than that in the control group, in 
which the ETS activities of the NBW pre-acclimated sludge reactors were 
also always higher than the corresponding DW group reactors. In the DW

tackling low metabolic activity issue under high salt concentrations. 
Gagliano et al. (2017) concluded that the addition of K+ (0.7 g/L) could 
alleviate the negative effect of high salinity (20 g Na+/L) on the biofilm 
formation and the performance of Up-flow Anaerobic Sludge Blanket 
(UASB) reactor. This observation also agrees with Wang et al. (2020b) 
who found that the methane yields from the corn straw were increased 
by 10% and 22% after the sludge being pre-augmented by N2-NBW and 
O2-NBW. 
3.3.2. Reduction of dissolved organic matters during the second stage 
Dissolved organic matters as the important intermediate products, 
including the soluble proteins, soluble carbohydrates, lactic acid, and 
individual VFAs, are monitored and showed in Fig. 5. During the first 6 
days, the concentration of soluble proteins was decreased slightly and 
then increased in the DW-9.0 and NBW-9.0. However, the concentra­
tions of soluble carbohydrates and lactic acid were decreased rapidly, 
especially in the NBW group, which was accompanied with a large 
accumulation of VFAs. As known, lactic acid is one of the main by- 
products in the anaerobic fermentation of FW, and its initial hydrolyt­
ic product is propionic acid (HPr), which is detrimental to methanogens 
(Cheng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2014). In this study, the higher accumu­
lation of lactic acid in the DW group (when compared to the NBW group) 
during the first stage led to the higher initial lactic acid concentration in 
the second stage (Fig. 5c). This would be accompanied with a higher HPr 
in the DW group, probably attributable to the lower methane yield in the 
DW group (Fig. 5d). On day 24, HPr was the dominant VFA in the DW 
group, about 1229.29 ± 15.39, 865.49 ± 0.83, 584.93 ± 28.63, and 
892.21 ± 11.57 mg/L in the DWcontrol-7.5, DW-7.5, DW-8.0, and DW- 
9.0; while acetic acid (HAc) dominated the NBW group, about 873.93 
± 22.88, 787.09 ± 75.45, 607.87 ± 34.13, and 202.75 ± 5.90 mg/L in 
the NBWcontrol-7.5, NBW-7.5, NBW-8.0, and NBW-9.0, respectively. 
Moreover, in the K+ added reactors, the degradation of organic 
matters was higher than that in the control group, suggesting the higher 
methane yield in the K+ added reactors which may be benefited from the 
rapid consumption of organic matters, especially VFAs. Li et al. (2018) 
found that at 2.0% NaCl condition the chemical oxygen demand (COD) 
removal efficiency, dehydrogenase activity, and the viability of micro­
organisms were enhanced by 115.4%, 77.2%, and 20.3% with the 
addition of KCl to AD of organic wastewater. Mu˜noz Sierra et al. (2018) 
also pointed out that a higher K+/Na+ ratio could achieve a higher COD 
removal efficiency and methane production rate when treating high 
saline phenolic wastewater, highlighting the importance of K+ to 
maintain the methanogenic activity under high salinity environment. 
3.3.3. Variations of pH and alkalinity during the second stage 
During the CH4 production stage, the initial pH was adjusted to 7.5, 
8.0, and 9.0 by using NaOH or KOH, which would inevitably cause the 
change of alkalinity during the process. Importantly, alkalinity is one of 
the key factors to maintain the stability of AD operation, which is a 
better indicator of imbalanced AD process than pH (Wang et al., 2018b). 
In addition, IA/PA and VFA/TA ratios are also commonly used as the 
preferable indicators that can monitor the methanogenic process (Sun 
et al., 2019). Therefore, the changes of pH, TA, IA/PA, and VFA/TA are 
recorded during the second stage (Fig. 6). The changes in pH were 
consistent with the results of VFAs accumulation and consumption, i.e., 
the pH dropped to the lowest when VFAs were largely accumulated, and 
then the pH was increased with the consumption of VFAs (Fig. 6a). 
Certainly, the system pH value returned to the optimum pH range 
(7.5–8.0) for the methanogens more quickly when a higher initial pH 
was adopted, and this phenomenon was more obvious in the DW group 
reactors. For instance, the pH values varied from 6.38, 6.48, 6.63, 6.85, 
6.51, 6.51, 6.73, and 6.82 to 6.9, 7.04, 7.12, 7.42, 7.45, 7.41, 7.51, and 
7.52 in the DWcontrol-7.5, DW-7.5, DW-8.0, DW-9.0, NBWcontrol-7.5,

NBW-7.5, NBW-8.0, and NBW-9.0 on day 6 to day 12, respectively. This 
observation indicates that addition of KOH plays a better pH regulating 
role in the DW group, which may be one of the reasons for the increase in 
methane production. The profiles of TA evolution are displayed in 
Fig. 6b. A more remarkable TA increase was noticed in the prophase of 
methane production in all the reactors, likely associated with the 
degradation of protein-rich substrates responsible for alkalinity pro­
duction (Adou et al., 2020). This observation agrees with the changes in 
the concentration of soluble protein, while the increase of TA was only 
825.83 and 938.44 mg CaCO3/L in the DW-9.0 and NBW-9.0 on day 6, 
which was lower than other reactors most probably due to the lower 
degradation of soluble proteins. However, the TA concentrations in both 
reactors were increased significantly after day 6, possibly due to the 
addition of a large number of alkaline matters (6 M KOH). 
According to previous studies, PA and IA can be used to distinguish 
the bicarbonate alkalinity and VFA alkalinity; and the IA/PA ratio is 
better for monitoring the buffering capacity of the AD process (Jantsch 
and Mattiasson, 2003; Sun et al., 2019). In the DWcontrol-7.5, the IA/PA 
ratio reached to 4.85 on day 6 (Fig. 6c), indicating its extreme instability 
because a sudden increase in the IA/PA ratio usually reflects a decrease 
in pH buffering capacity (Banks et al., 2012). Interestingly, the IA/PA 
ratio in the NBW group with the addition of KOH were lower than that in 
the corresponding DW group. This indicates that the buffering capacity 
of the NBW group was higher than the DW group. As the AD progressed, 
the IA/PA ratios continued to decline in all reactors, which were 
decreased to 0.25, 0.24, 0.24, 0.20, 0.17, 0.13, 0.08, and 0.16. in the 
DWcontrol-7.5, DW-7.5, DW-8.0, DW-9.0, NBWcontrol-7.5, NBW-7.5, 
NBW-8.0, and NBW-9.0 at the end of the second stage, respectively. 
This observation implies that the reactors gradually recovered and 
became stable. Similarly, the VFA/TA ratio showed an increase trend at 
first and then decreased in all reactors (Fig. 6d). Liu et al. (2019a) 
summarized the range of VFA/TA ratios for the stable operation of AD 
for methane production from different substrates. According to their 
results, the VFA/TA ratio of < 0.4 signals a stable co-digestion of waste 
activated sludge and FW or co-digestion of sewage sludge and fruit 
wastes; however, the VFA/TA ratio of 0.59 may reflect a stable operation 
of the mono-digestion of FW. In this study, the VFA/TA ratios were 
lower than 0.5 in all reactors after day 12, suggesting that combination 
of Air-NBW pre-acclimation and K+ supplementation could better 
maintain the pH buffer capacity during the second stage for CH4 pro­
duction from high saline FW. 
3.3.4. Changes of TAN and FAN during the second stage 
For the protein-rich substrates, ammonia nitrogen would be released 
due to the decomposition of proteins, amino acids, urea, and nucleic 
acids. Considering the addition of KOH in the methanogenic stage to 
supplement the alkalinity, the conversion of TAN to FAN in a slightly 
alkaline environment is known as one of the inhibitors to methanogens 
(Sposob et al., 2020). Thus, the concentrations of TAN and FAN are 
summarized (Table 3). The TAN and FAN concentrations in the NBW 
group were slightly higher than those in the corresponding DW group, 
and the increase in FAN was more obvious in the DW-9.0 and NBW-9.0 
reactors because FAN is mainly affected by TAN, pH, and temperature 
according to Eq. (1). Many previous studies have disclosed the inhibition 
effects of TAN and FAN on AD, but it is difficult to determine the limit 
concentration of TAN or FAN to methane production inhibition. Bi et al. 
(2020) reported that > 3000 mg N/L of TAN would cause reduced 
methane production and toxicity to methanogens. Dai et al. (2016) and 
Westerholm et al. (2011), however, found that the methanogenic ac­
tivity was affected only when the TAN concentration was higher than 
5000 mg N/L. In any case, the concentration of TAN in this study (al­
ways < 1700 mg N/L) was far lower than the inhibition concentrations 
as mentioned above, thus no inhibition on methane production was 
observed.

3.4. Application potential 
The research of NBW in the field of AD is becoming a hotspot, 
however, there are still numerous challenges in practical applications, 
including increase in the AD reactor volume due to the addition of NBW. 
This study tried to use Air-NBW to pre-acclimate anaerobically digested 
sludge that was used as inoculum in the two-stage AD of high salinity 
FW. On the one hand, results showed that Air-NBW pre-acclimated 
sludge can significantly enhance the H2 and CH4 production, and the 
reactor volume could be reduced compared with adding Air-NBW 
directly. On the other hand, the reactor start-up at each stage was 
accelerated under the high salinity by using Ari-NBW pre-acclimated 
sludge as inoculum. In addition, from an economic perspective, 
substituting KOH for NaOH in the methanogenic stage to adjust the 
initial pH would not increase the cost because it is normally necessary to 
adjust the pH in the second stage of the two-stage AD of FW. Compared 
with the addition of KCl to mitigate the inhibition of salt on metha­

4. Conclusions 
This study investigated the performance of two-stage AD of high 
saline (20 g NaCl/L) FW by using Air-NBW pre-acclimated anaerobically 
digested sludge and the effects of K+ addition on methanogenic stage by 
adding KOH to adjust the initial pH. Results indicate that the H2 yield 
increased about 46% in the NBW group, and the addition of KOH also 
enhanced the CH4 yield and ETS activity in the second stage. Addi­
tionally, a shorter start-up period and more stable performance were 
obtained in the NBW group with the KOH addition, especially in NBW- 
8.0, in addition to improved fertilizer value of the digestate.
